sql-basics.heading: Data types and constraints
body: Every column has a type, and choosing it well prevents whole classes of bugs. Use integer types for counts and identifiers, `DECIMAL(10,2)` or `NUMERIC` for money (never floating point, which cannot store 0.10 exactly), `VARCHAR(n)` or `TEXT` for strings, `DATE` and `TIMESTAMP` for time, and `BOOLEAN` where the database supports it. Store dates as dates, not as text, so sorting and date arithmetic work.

Constraints let the database enforce rules no matter which application writes the data. `PRIMARY KEY` identifies each row, `FOREIGN KEY` ensures a referenced row exists, `NOT NULL` requires a value, `UNIQUE` prevents duplicates such as two accounts with one email, and `CHECK (price >= 0)` rejects impossible values. Exact type names and behaviours vary between PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and SQLite, so check your database's documentation.

sql-select.heading: Pattern matching, ranges and NULL-safe filters
body: Beyond equality, a few operators cover most filters. `BETWEEN 10 AND 20` is inclusive of both ends. `IN ('UK', 'IE', 'FR')` replaces a chain of ORs. `LIKE 'Ana%'` matches values starting with 'Ana', `%` standing for any run of characters and `_` for exactly one; a leading wildcard such as `LIKE '%son'` usually prevents the database from using an index. Case sensitivity of LIKE depends on the database and collation.

NULL needs its own care. `WHERE discount <> 10` silently excludes rows where discount is NULL, because comparisons with NULL are unknown, not true. Write `WHERE discount <> 10 OR discount IS NULL` when you mean to include them, or use `COALESCE(discount, 0)` to substitute a default. `CASE WHEN total > 100 THEN 'large' ELSE 'small' END` derives labels in the select list.

sql-aggregates.heading: Common grouping mistakes
body: Every column in the select list must either appear in `GROUP BY` or be inside an aggregate. `SELECT customer_id, city, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id` is an error in PostgreSQL and SQL Server because `city` has no single value per group; MySQL may accept it and return an arbitrary city, which hides the bug. Group by every non-aggregated column, or aggregate it.

Watch for NULL and duplicates. `COUNT(*)` counts rows, `COUNT(email)` counts non-NULL emails, and `AVG(rating)` ignores NULL ratings rather than treating them as zero. Joining before aggregating can multiply rows, so a customer with three orders and two addresses produces six joined rows and inflated sums. Aggregate in a subquery or CTE first, then join the totals.

sql-joins.heading: Other join types and set thinking
body: `RIGHT JOIN` is a LEFT JOIN written the other way round, and most people rewrite it as a LEFT JOIN for readability. `FULL OUTER JOIN` keeps unmatched rows from both sides, which is useful for reconciling two lists: rows with NULL on one side exist in only one list. `CROSS JOIN` pairs every row with every other row; it is occasionally useful for generating combinations, and accidentally created by a missing ON condition.

To find rows with no match, use a LEFT JOIN and test the right side for NULL, or `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)`. Avoid `NOT IN` with a subquery that can return NULL: if any value is NULL, `NOT IN` returns no rows at all. Always join on the full key, and check row counts before and after joining.

sql-ddl-dml.heading: Changing schemas safely
body: `ALTER TABLE` changes a live table: `ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR(30);` is usually quick, but adding a NOT NULL column with a computed default, changing a type, or adding an index on a large table can lock it or rewrite it entirely. Check how your database handles each operation, and run large changes in a maintenance window or with online tools such as `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` in PostgreSQL.

Keep schema changes in version-controlled migration files (Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic, Rails migrations), applied in order to every environment, so development, test and production never drift. Make changes backward compatible in steps: add the new column, deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, and only then drop the old column. `UPSERT` (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` in PostgreSQL, `MERGE` in SQL Server) handles insert-or-update in one statement.

sql-subqueries.heading: Recursive CTEs and choosing the right tool
body: A recursive CTE walks hierarchies such as an org chart or a category tree. It has an anchor query that selects the starting rows and a recursive part that joins back to the CTE: `WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (SELECT id, manager_id, name FROM staff WHERE id = 42 UNION ALL SELECT s.id, s.manager_id, s.name FROM staff s JOIN chain c ON s.id = c.manager_id) SELECT * FROM chain;` lists an employee and every manager above them. Recursion stops when the recursive part returns no rows.

Subqueries, CTEs and joins can often express the same question. Prefer a join when you need columns from both tables, `EXISTS` when you only need to know whether a match exists, and a CTE when naming an intermediate step makes the query easier to read. Check performance with `EXPLAIN` rather than assuming one form is faster.

sql-indexes-norm.heading: Composite indexes and when to denormalise
body: An index on several columns is used from the left. An index on `(customer_id, created_at)` serves `WHERE customer_id = 42` and `WHERE customer_id = 42 AND created_at > '2026-01-01'`, but not `WHERE created_at > '2026-01-01'` alone. Put the column used for equality first and the range column second. An index that contains every column a query needs (a covering index) lets the database answer without reading the table.

Normalisation to third normal form is the right default for transactional systems. Reporting and analytics systems often denormalise on purpose, for example a star schema with a wide fact table and dimension tables, or a stored order total, because reads vastly outnumber writes. Denormalise deliberately, and keep the copies consistent with triggers, scheduled jobs or materialised views.

sql-transactions-security.heading: Isolation levels and preventing SQL injection
body: Isolation levels decide what concurrent transactions can see. Read committed, the default in PostgreSQL and SQL Server, prevents dirty reads but allows a row to change between two reads in the same transaction. Repeatable read prevents that, and serializable makes concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one at a time, at the cost of more conflicts that the application must retry. Choose the weakest level that keeps your data correct.

SQL injection happens when user input is concatenated into query text. The fix is parameterised queries in every language, for example `cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = %s", (email,))`, never string formatting. Back it up with least-privilege database accounts for each application, no administrative accounts in application connection strings, and input validation as a second layer.

docker-basics.heading: How containers are isolated
body: A container is an ordinary Linux process with restricted views of the system. Namespaces give it its own process IDs, network interfaces, mount points and hostname, so it sees only its own processes and files. Control groups (cgroups) limit how much CPU, memory and I/O it can use. Because containers share the host's kernel, they start in milliseconds and use little memory, but they are not as strongly isolated as virtual machines.

That shared kernel matters for security and portability. A kernel vulnerability can let a process escape its container, and Linux containers need a Linux kernel: Docker Desktop on Windows and macOS runs them inside a lightweight Linux VM. When strong isolation between tenants is required, use VMs, or sandboxed runtimes such as gVisor or Kata Containers.

docker-images.heading: Writing a good Dockerfile
body: Pin the base image to a specific version, such as `python:3.12-slim`, rather than `latest`, so builds are reproducible. Add a `.dockerignore` file listing `.git`, `node_modules`, test data and secrets, so they are never sent to the build or copied into the image. Combine related commands into one `RUN` and clean up in the same step, for example `apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*`, because files deleted in a later layer still take up space in an earlier one.

Know the difference between `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT`: `ENTRYPOINT` sets the executable and `CMD` supplies default arguments that `docker run` can override. Use the exec form (`["python", "app.py"]`) so the process receives signals and stops cleanly. Never pass secrets with `ARG` or `ENV`, which are visible in the image history; use BuildKit secret mounts (`RUN --mount=type=secret`) instead.

docker-run.heading: Container lifecycle and cleanup
body: A container moves through created, running, paused, stopped and removed states. `docker stop` sends SIGTERM and, after a grace period (10 seconds by default), SIGKILL, so applications should handle SIGTERM and shut down cleanly. `docker kill` sends SIGKILL immediately. A stopped container keeps its writable layer until you remove it, which is why `docker ps -a` often shows a long list of exited containers.

Clean up regularly: `docker container prune` removes stopped containers, `docker image prune` removes dangling images, and `docker system df` shows how much space images, containers, volumes and build cache use. `docker system prune -a --volumes` removes everything unused, including volumes, so read its warning before running it on a machine with data you need.

docker-data-net.heading: Backing up volumes and publishing ports safely
body: Volumes live outside the container, so they need their own backups. A common method mounts the volume into a temporary container and archives it: `docker run --rm -v pgdata:/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine tar czf /backup/pgdata.tgz -C /data .`. For databases, prefer the database's own dump tool (`pg_dump`, `mysqldump`) so the backup is consistent rather than a copy of files being written.

Publishing a port with `-p 8080:80` binds to every host interface by default, making the service reachable from the network. Bind to `127.0.0.1:8080:80` for services only the host should reach. Also note that Docker writes its own iptables rules for published ports, which can bypass host firewall rules such as ufw; check what is actually exposed with `ss -tlnp` and a scan from another machine.

docker-compose.heading: Environments, overrides and secrets in Compose
body: Compose reads variables from a `.env` file in the project directory and substitutes them into `compose.yaml`, for example `image: myapp:${APP_VERSION}`. Per-environment differences go in override files: `compose.override.yaml` is merged automatically for local development, and `docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d` applies production settings. `docker compose config` prints the final merged configuration, which is the quickest way to check what will run.

Keep secrets out of the YAML and out of version control. Compose supports a `secrets:` section that mounts files at `/run/secrets/<name>` inside the container, which many official images read through `_FILE` variables such as `POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE`. Profiles (`profiles: [debug]`) let optional services such as admin tools start only when requested with `--profile debug`.

docker-registry.heading: Signing, scanning and retention
body: Before deployment, scan images for known vulnerabilities with tools such as Trivy, Grype or the registry's built-in scanner, and fail the pipeline on critical findings that have a fix. Generate a software bill of materials (SBOM) so you can answer 'which images contain this vulnerable library?' when the next major CVE is announced.

Signing proves an image came from your pipeline and has not been altered. Sigstore's cosign signs an image digest and stores the signature in the registry, and admission policies in Kubernetes can refuse unsigned images. Set retention rules in the registry to delete old untagged images, and make release tags immutable where the registry supports it, so `app:1.4.2` always means the same image.

docker-optimization-security.heading: Hardening at run time
body: Image hardening is half the job; the run options decide what a compromised container can do. Drop all Linux capabilities and add back only what is needed (`--cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE`), prevent privilege escalation with `--security-opt no-new-privileges`, make the root filesystem read-only with a tmpfs for scratch space, and set memory, CPU and PID limits. Never use `--privileged` for application containers.

Never mount the Docker socket (`/var/run/docker.sock`) into an application container: whoever controls the socket controls the host. Rootless mode runs the Docker daemon itself as an unprivileged user, and user namespace remapping maps root inside the container to an unprivileged user on the host. Docker Bench for Security checks a host against the CIS Docker Benchmark.

docker-ops.heading: Logging and monitoring containers
body: Applications in containers should log to standard output and standard error; Docker captures those streams and `docker logs` reads them. The default json-file driver keeps logs on the host with no size limit unless you set one, so configure rotation in `/etc/docker/daemon.json` (`"log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"}`) or ship logs to a central system with a driver such as fluentd, or an agent that reads the files.

`docker stats` shows live CPU, memory, network and I/O per container, and `docker events` streams lifecycle events such as restarts and out-of-memory kills. For anything beyond one host, export metrics (cAdvisor with Prometheus is a common pairing) and alert on restart loops, memory near the limit and failing health checks.

k8s-basics.heading: Working with kubectl and contexts
body: kubectl reads its connection details from a kubeconfig file (`~/.kube/config` by default), which can hold several clusters, users and namespaces combined into contexts. `kubectl config get-contexts` lists them and `kubectl config use-context staging` switches; checking the current context before running a destructive command prevents changes to the wrong cluster. `kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=shop` sets a default namespace.

A few flags make kubectl far more useful: `-o wide` adds node and IP columns, `-o yaml` shows the full object as stored, `-l app=web` filters by label, and `--dry-run=client -o yaml` prints the manifest a command would create without creating it, a quick way to generate starting YAML. `kubectl api-resources` lists every resource type the cluster supports.

k8s-workloads.heading: Multi-container pods and pod lifecycle
body: Most pods run one application container, but helpers are common. Init containers run to completion before the app starts, for example to wait for a database or run a migration. Sidecar containers run alongside the app for the pod's lifetime, such as a log shipper or service-mesh proxy; Kubernetes 1.29+ supports native sidecars as init containers with `restartPolicy: Always`, so they start before and stop after the main container.

A pod's phase moves from Pending (scheduled, pulling images) to Running, and ends as Succeeded or Failed. Common problems show in the container status: `ImagePullBackOff` means the image name, tag or registry credentials are wrong; `CrashLoopBackOff` means the container keeps exiting; `OOMKilled` means it exceeded its memory limit. `kubectl describe pod` shows these with the events that explain them.

k8s-config.heading: Labels, selectors and managing manifests
body: Labels are key-value pairs that tie Kubernetes objects together. A Deployment's selector picks its pods by label, a Service routes to pods by label, and a NetworkPolicy applies to pods by label, so a typo in a label silently breaks the connection. Use a consistent set, such as the recommended `app.kubernetes.io/name`, `app.kubernetes.io/version` and `app.kubernetes.io/component`. Annotations hold non-identifying metadata such as build information.

Apply manifests declaratively with `kubectl apply -f dir/`, and keep them in Git so every change is reviewed. `kubectl diff -f dir/` shows what would change before you apply. For variation between environments, Kustomize (built into kubectl with `-k`) layers patches over a base, and Helm packages manifests as templated charts with values files.

k8s-networking.heading: Controlling traffic with NetworkPolicy
body: By default every pod can talk to every other pod in the cluster, across namespaces. A NetworkPolicy restricts that: once any policy selects a pod for ingress, only traffic the policies allow can reach it. A common pattern is a default-deny policy per namespace (`podSelector: {}` with `policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]` and no rules), followed by policies that allow specific flows, such as the web pods to the API pods on port 8080, and DNS egress to kube-system.

NetworkPolicy is enforced by the network plugin, not by Kubernetes itself, so it only works with a CNI that supports it, such as Calico or Cilium. Test policies after applying them: `kubectl exec` into a pod and try to reach a service that should be blocked. The Gateway API is the successor to Ingress for routing external traffic, with richer routing and clearer roles.

k8s-storage.heading: StatefulSets, snapshots and data safety
body: For databases and other stateful workloads, a StatefulSet uses `volumeClaimTemplates` to give each replica its own PersistentVolumeClaim (`data-db-0`, `data-db-1`), and the claim follows the pod's stable name if it is rescheduled. Scaling down does not delete those claims, so the data is still there when you scale back up.

Check the StorageClass reclaim policy: `Delete` removes the underlying disk when the claim is deleted, and `Retain` keeps it for manual recovery. For production data, use `Retain` or make sure backups exist. VolumeSnapshots (with a CSI driver that supports them) take point-in-time copies, and tools such as Velero back up both Kubernetes objects and volume data to object storage. Running a production database in Kubernetes is possible, but a managed database service is often simpler.

k8s-deployments.heading: Tuning rollouts and protecting availability
body: A Deployment's rolling update is controlled by `maxSurge` (how many extra pods may be created above the desired count) and `maxUnavailable` (how many may be missing). `maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0` adds a new pod before removing an old one, keeping full capacity at the cost of extra resources. `minReadySeconds` makes Kubernetes wait until a new pod has been ready for a while before continuing, which catches pods that crash shortly after starting.

A PodDisruptionBudget protects availability during voluntary disruptions such as node drains: `minAvailable: 2` stops a drain from evicting pods if fewer than two would remain. For riskier releases, canary and blue-green strategies send a small share of traffic to the new version first; tools such as Argo Rollouts or a service mesh automate them with automatic rollback on errors.

k8s-operations.heading: Observability for clusters
body: `kubectl top pods` and `kubectl top nodes` show current CPU and memory use, provided the metrics-server is installed. For history and alerting, most clusters run Prometheus to collect metrics from the kubelet, kube-state-metrics and applications, with Grafana dashboards and alert rules for symptoms such as pods restarting, nodes not ready, persistent volumes filling and Deployments with unavailable replicas.

Container logs disappear when a pod is deleted, so ship them off the node with an agent such as Fluent Bit running as a DaemonSet. `kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp` gives a quick timeline of what the cluster has been doing. For a crashed container, `kubectl logs <pod> --previous` shows the output of the last failed run, and `kubectl debug` attaches an ephemeral debugging container to a running pod.

k8s-security.heading: Securing the cluster itself
body: Protect the control plane: keep the API server private or restricted to known networks, authenticate users through an identity provider (OIDC) rather than shared certificates, enable audit logging, and encrypt Secrets at rest in etcd, ideally with a KMS provider. Keep Kubernetes and node images patched; minor versions receive upstream patches for about 14 months.

Limit what workloads can reach. Disable automatic service-account token mounting for pods that do not call the API (`automountServiceAccountToken: false`), and never bind `cluster-admin` to application accounts. Admission policies, through ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper, can block privileged pods, images from untrusted registries and missing resource limits. The CIS Kubernetes Benchmark, checked with kube-bench, gives a full checklist.

git-basics.heading: Configuring Git and ignoring files
body: Before your first commit, tell Git who you are: `git config --global user.name "Ana Silva"` and `git config --global user.email ana@example.com`. These details are recorded in every commit. Other useful settings include `git config --global init.defaultBranch main` and a default editor for commit messages. `git config --list --show-origin` shows every setting and the file it came from.

A `.gitignore` file lists patterns Git should never track: build output (`dist/`, `*.o`), dependencies (`node_modules/`), editor files and, above all, secrets such as `.env`. Add it at the start of a project; ignoring a file that is already committed does not remove it from history. `git check-ignore -v file` explains which rule ignores a file, and gitignore.io-style templates give sensible starting lists per language.

git-staging-commits.heading: Writing good commit messages
body: A commit message is a note to a future reader, often yourself, trying to understand why the code changed. A widely used convention is a short summary line of about 50 characters in the imperative mood ('Fix rounding in invoice totals', not 'Fixed stuff'), a blank line, then a body that explains why the change was needed and anything non-obvious about how. The diff already shows what changed.

Keep each commit to one logical change, so it can be reviewed, reverted or cherry-picked on its own. Some teams adopt Conventional Commits (`feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`), which lets tools generate changelogs and version numbers automatically. Before committing, read `git diff --staged` once more; it is the cheapest review there is, and it catches debugging code and secrets.

git-remotes.heading: Authentication, forks and keeping in sync
body: Remotes are reached over HTTPS or SSH. HTTPS uses a personal access token or a credential manager rather than your account password; SSH uses a key pair, with the public key added to your hosting account. `git remote -v` shows each remote's URL, and `git remote set-url origin git@github.com:org/repo.git` switches a clone from HTTPS to SSH.

When contributing to a project you cannot push to, you fork it and clone your fork as `origin`, then add the original as `upstream`: `git remote add upstream https://github.com/org/repo.git`. To stay current, `git fetch upstream` and merge or rebase `upstream/main` into your branch. `git push --force-with-lease` is the safe way to update a branch after rebasing: it refuses if someone else pushed in the meantime.

git-branching.heading: Inspecting and tidying branches
body: `git branch -vv` lists local branches with their last commit and the remote branch each one tracks, including how far ahead or behind it is. `git branch --merged main` shows branches whose work is already in main and can be deleted with `git branch -d`. `-D` forces deletion of unmerged work, so use it only when you are sure. `git fetch --prune` removes remote-tracking branches that were deleted on the server.

`git log --oneline --graph --all` draws the whole branch structure in the terminal, which helps when you are unsure where a branch started or what a merge will bring in. `git log main..feature` lists commits on feature that are not yet in main, and `git diff main...feature` shows the changes the feature branch introduced since it diverged.

git-conflicts.heading: Tools that make conflicts easier
body: Setting `git config --global merge.conflictstyle zdiff3` adds a third section to conflict markers showing the common ancestor's version, which makes it much easier to see what each side changed. `git mergetool` opens a configured visual merge tool, and most editors, including VS Code, show conflicts with buttons to accept either side or both. After resolving, run the tests before committing: a conflict-free merge can still produce broken code.

If you resolve the same conflict repeatedly, for example while rebasing a long-running branch, enable rerere (`git config --global rerere.enabled true`), which records how you resolved a conflict and reapplies it automatically next time. Conflicts are fewer and smaller when branches are short-lived and merged often.

git-undo.heading: Choosing the safest undo
body: Before undoing anything, check whether the commits have been pushed. Local, unpushed history can be rewritten freely with `git reset`, `git commit --amend` or an interactive rebase. Shared history should not be rewritten, because collaborators' copies still contain the old commits; use `git revert`, which adds a new commit that undoes the change, and works even for merges with `git revert -m 1 <merge>`.

`git reset` has three modes. `--soft` moves the branch but keeps your changes staged, `--mixed` (the default) keeps them unstaged, and `--hard` discards them. Uncommitted work lost to `--hard` is very hard to recover, so stash or commit first. To recover a single file from an older commit, `git restore --source=<commit> path/to/file` is precise and leaves everything else alone.

git-workflows.heading: Protecting the main branch
body: Whatever workflow a team uses, the main branch should always be releasable. Hosting platforms enforce this with branch protection rules: require pull requests instead of direct pushes, require at least one approving review, require CI checks to pass, and require branches to be up to date before merging. A CODEOWNERS file routes reviews of sensitive paths, such as infrastructure or authentication code, to the right people automatically.

Agree how pull requests are merged. A merge commit preserves every commit and the branch shape; squash merging collapses a branch into one commit on main, giving a tidy history; rebase merging replays the commits in a straight line. Many teams squash by default. Signed commits and tags (GPG or SSH signing) let reviewers verify who authored a change.

git-internals-hygiene.heading: Large files, secrets and repository maintenance
body: Git stores every version of every file forever, so large binary files make clones slow and repositories huge. Git LFS stores large files such as images, models and datasets on a separate server and keeps only small pointer files in the repository. Track patterns with `git lfs track "*.psd"` before committing them.

If a secret is committed, treat it as compromised and revoke it immediately; then remove it from history with `git filter-repo` (the recommended replacement for `git filter-branch`) or BFG, and force-push, knowing that existing clones and forks still hold the old history. Prevent it next time with a pre-commit secret scanner such as gitleaks. `git gc` packs objects and cleans up, and `git fsck` checks the repository's integrity.
